content.title: Thorough experiments, while weak technical novelty
content.review:
This paper aims to solve the problem of sensor image super-resolution with references from other modality. It uses a deformation network to handle the misalignment between the LR image and the RGB input, and then integrate the feature of the deformation-corrected RGB image with the feature map of the upsampled input to generate the final output.

## Pros
- This paper addresses an interesting while less-explored question in super-resolution.
- The experiment is quite thorough. It shows results on NIR, depth images, and also the single modality experiments.
- The joint training of deformation network and the main network is interesting. Thinking about the whole framework is only trained with SR reconstruction loss, the alignment result in Fig.9 is inspiring too. 
- Good quantitative and qualitative results.

## Cons
- The technical novelty of network design is marginal. 
- The part of self-supervised training could be better explained. For example, the appendix mentioned the runtime changes depending on the required iterations --- What's the stopping criteria? How about comparing this with ZSSR? 
- Besides, there are some minor issues: most of the visual results come without LR inputs; some misuse of "x" and "$\times$", etc.

## Additional questions
1. The inference time is rather long, probably due to most of the operations are in the high resolution domain. I am curious about whether the author try to to the align / feature aggregation in LR domain? How would the result be like?
2. I am also curious about the robustness and functionality of the RGB reference. Has the author tried to use non-related images, or even blank image? To what extent will the result be influenced?

Overall, this paper is interesting to read for me. Thanks for the author to illustrate this question with rich experimental results. Still, I have some concerns on the method design, robustness and other details. Thus, I would give this score for now. Feedback from the author is greatly appreciated.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: We would like to thank Reviewer3 for his positive and constructive feedback

content.title: We would like to thank Reviewer3 for his positive and constructive feedback
content.comment:
As for the technical novelty, our opinion was stated in the answers to the other reviewers

> The part of self-supervised training could be better explained. For example, the appendix mentioned the runtime changes depending on the required iterations --- What's the stopping criteria? How about comparing this with ZSSR?

We take this criticism and decide to include more training details. We generally stop when the slope of our reconstruction error (which is identical to our loss, but taken on the full image and not on a single patch) remains unchanged for a fixed number of iterations. This is similar to ZSSR

> I am also curious about the robustness and functionality of the RGB reference. Has the author tried to use non-related images, or even blank image? To what extent will the result be influenced?

Using a blank image causes the RGB features to zero out quickly, as expected. This was tested by us but not included in the paper since it is mostly trivial. Using a completely unrelated image was also tested and behaves the same way. Using an RGB image with some redundant details is the interesting experiment since it evaluates our abilities to ignore only some of the RGB information and use the relevant information. Our method does that successfully, as shown in figure 2. It surpasses ZSSR while utilizing only the relevant RGB information, and avoiding adding the respective artifacts where the redundant object appeared.

content.title: Weak Reject
content.review:
In this paper, the authors propose a single-pair approach for Cross-Modality Super-Resolution, which uses an RGB image of a high-resolution to increase the resolution of a low-resolution modality. The network is internally trained in a self-supervised manner and contains a deformation model to align details from RGB image to the target modality in a coarse-to-fine manner. Experiment results indicate the proposed method produces state-of-the-art super-resolved images, which also allows the two modalities to be moderately misaligned.

----Strengths:
1.	The authors focus on the cross-modality super-resolution problem. The research direction of it is meaningful. The proposed network could allow the two modalities to be moderately misaligned, which is more effective in processing the cross-modality super-resolution problem in real-world scenarios. 

----Weaknesses: 
1.	Generally, this paper focus on addressing the cross-modality super-resolution problem in real-world scenarios. To achieve this, the proposed method contains a deformation model to align details from the two input images. Besides, the network is trained in a self-supervised manner. However, the methods (deformation convolution, self-supervised) are standard. In its current form, the contribution of this paper is not significant enough for ICLR. In fact, an application conference would be a more suitable venue
2.	From the abstract, “traditional state-of-the-arts which are trained on external datasets often struggle with yielding an artifact-free result that is still loyal to the target modality characteristics.” From the introduction, “they tend to fuse redundant details from the guiding modality anyway, resulting in the addition of textures and artifacts to the lower resolution modality” However, on the algorithm side, it is not clear why the proposed method could alleviate this problem. The justification needs to be articulated more clearly in the paper 
3.	In the experiment part, can you provide more implementation and training details about this work?  For example, what is the “Feature-Extractor I” and the “Feature-Extractor 2”?
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: We would like to thank Reviewer2 for his constructive feedback

content.title: We would like to thank Reviewer2 for his constructive feedback
content.comment:
We thank reviewer 2 for his constructive feedback.

> However, the methods (deformation convolution, self-supervised) are standard. In its current form, the contribution of this paper is not significant

While it is true that the inner sub-components are not inherently new, the way we combine them together to form a self-supervised framework is definitely novel, since it enables the framework to surpass state-of-the-arts while not requiring a dataset. We believe that performance and applicability are more important than the internal complexity of the modules, especially in an era when many works are too complex to implement and train

> From the abstract, “traditional state-of-the-arts which are trained on external datasets often struggle with yielding an artifact-free result that is still loyal to the target modality characteristics.” From the introduction, “they tend to fuse redundant details from the guiding modality anyway, resulting in the addition of textures and artifacts to the lower resolution modality” However, on the algorithm side, it is not clear why the proposed method could alleviate this problem. The justification needs to be articulated more clearly in the paper

A high-level explanation is found in the beginning of chapter 3 and in the intro - externally trained methods, trained on a full dataset, have hard time generalizing, since **it is hard to train a network to infer** (at testing time) which RGB details should be incorporated and which not. It might have seen 200 pairs where a RGB car textures should be incorporated to improve the output sharpness, and other 200 pairs where RGB car textures are irrelevant to the final output. Therefore, the task of this network is much more complex. **Our network sees only the single input pair and therefore adjusts** (as stated many times in the paper) to the specifics - if adding RGB car textures help minimize the loss it would do so, and if not it would avoid them.

> In the experiment part, can you provide more implementation and training details about this work? For example, what is the “Feature-Extractor I” and the “Feature-Extractor 2”?

The implementation details (for example, the structure and layers of Feature-Extractor 1/2), activations and learning rates are all specified in Appendix A1.2 and referred to from the original paper. The training details are covered in chapter 3.2.

content.title: My biggest concern is technical novelty. If the author’s can convincingly explain their technical novelty in the rebuttal, it would be helpful.
content.review:
Imaging hardware that is not rgb is more expensive than rgb sensors while the resolution is lower.
It is natural to think of a way to super resolve the low res sensor leveraging the rgb sensor which has the higher resolution information. 
This paper is about performing SR on low res non-rgb images, using the knowledge from rgb image. 
Fusing images from different modalities is difficult because of different innate properties. 
The authors propose a single pair approach to cross modality SR. 
the network is trained on a single two image pair. 

This work is a nice work, which addresses a practical need and a simple solution to solve it. The solution is not impractical nor requires much supervised data. 
The approach is understandable and the design choices are understandable as well. It is pretty much straight forward. 
This work deserves a good publication. However, I’m not sure it meets the bar of ICLR. 
The novelty of this paper in terms of learning representations, is limited in my opinion. 
This work has a sound problem definition and solution. The architecture however does not provide additional insights into learning representation, but rather uses known and popular network components. 
This work is application prone and provides a working solution, which might be more suited to other conference venues. 

Minor comment: please align Table 1.

In short, my biggest concern is technical novelty. If the author’s can convincingly explain their technical novelty in the rebuttal, it would be helpful.

content.comment:
As for our novelty, we believe that the performance and applicability of a method is more valueable than its internal complexity. We view simple architecture as an advantage, since applicability is one recurring issue among works that are too complex to implement and/or train.

We present a method that surpasses state-of-the-arts from top tier conferences (ECCV, ICCV, CVPR) while eliminating the need for a dataset. While it is true that the inner sub-components are not inherently new, the way we combine them together to form a self-supervised framework is definitely novel. One can argue that our architecture is relatively simple, but if its performance is good enough to surpass state-of-the-arts, then it meets, in our opinion the required bar.

content.title: A cross-modality super resolution method with weak experiments
content.review:
The authors present a single-pair method for cross-modality super-resolution. The method relies on input pair of images. Similar idea has been published in previous works, limiting the novelty of the paper.

The experiments are not extensive or convincing. The authors should have compared with methods, which don’t use RGB images as guidance. Such comparisons would show how much the introduction of another modality data could improve.

In abstract, the authors claim that ‘We show that CMSR produces state-of-the-art super resolved images, yet without introducing artifacts or irrelevant details that originate from the RGB image only.’. However, there lacks corresponding visual results to support this claim.

The quality of most figures are relatively low and should be improved heavily. There appears obvious compression artifacts in the figures.

The writing and paper organization should also be improved largely. For example, Table 1 even exceeds the paper width, which is not a good shape for top conferences.

display_title: We would like to thank Reviewer1 for his constructive feedback

content.title: We would like to thank Reviewer1 for his constructive feedback
content.comment:
We would like to thank Reviewer1 for his constructive feedback.

> The experiments are not extensive or convincing. The authors should have compared with methods, which don’t use RGB images as guidance. Such comparisons would show how much the introduction of another modality data could improve.

We compared against ZSSR (CVPR'18), who doesn't use the guiding modality, both visually and numerically throughout the paper, as it is also a self-supervised single image SR and serves as our baseline model. Our visual/numerical advantage shows the contribution of the RGB modality, whose residual is also given in figure 6. Comparing against dataset-based single-modality SR method would diverge too much our setup, as the inputs are different and the training is inherently different. We show our advantage against multiple cross-modality methods, including state-of-the-arts from ECCV'16 and ICCV'19.

> In abstract, the authors claim that ‘We show that CMSR produces state-of-the-art super resolved images, yet without introducing artifacts or irrelevant details that originate from the RGB image only.’. However, there lacks corresponding visual results to support this claim.

This is shown explicitly in figures 2 and 14, and implicitly in figure 10 which contains a thorough evaluation where it is possible to see clearly that our method avoids RGB artifacts.

> The writing and paper organization should also be improved largely. For example, Table 1 even exceeds the paper width, which is not a good shape for top conferences.

While it is true that the layout of the paper should be touched up before it is published (as encouraged by ICLR), we don't believe an exceeding Table should define how well the paper is written, and impact its scoring.



As for novelty, we believe that improving upon state-of-the-arts while eliminating the need for a full dataset is novel. even if the sub-components of our method are not inherently new, the way we combine them together to form a fully differentiable framework is definitely novel.
